fieldFixes.contribution: In the late 1980s and early 1990s Poulsen was a notorious hacker: a 1993 federal indictment accused him of seizing control of the incoming phone lines of Los Angeles radio stations, by hacking Pacific Bell's computers, to win their contests, and of setting up his own wiretaps. He pleaded guilty, including to breaking into a computer for the names of FBI undercover businesses. He became a journalist and Wired's investigations editor, and in 2011 asked Aaron Swartz to build an open-source anonymous in-box for sources. After Swartz's death he launched it as Strongbox at The New Yorker in May 2013 and handed it to the Freedom of the Press Foundation, which renamed it SecureDrop, in October 2013.
fieldFixes.thread: A former intruder once charged with setting up his own wiretaps, Poulsen co-developed a system in which the recipient cannot learn who the sender is — protection that does not depend on the organisation's goodwill.

issues: The contribution gets the order wrong. It says Snowden 'gave journalists top-secret documents ... then flew to Hong Kong on 20 May 2013'. The cited Guardian article says that 'At the NSA office in Hawaii where he was working, he copied the last set of documents he intended to disclose', then 'On May 20, he boarded a flight to Hong Kong'. It also says the journalists identified him 'after several days of interviews' there. The main handover to Greenwald and Poitras happened in Hong Kong in June, not before the flight. Reworded so the text no longer puts the handover before the flight.

The influence overstates the USA FREEDOM Act. The record says the Act 'stopped bulk collection'. The Ninth Circuit says it 'effectively ended the NSA’s bulk telephony metadata collection program', and the Act's Sec. 103 is a 'Prohibition on bulk collection of tangible things'. Other bulk programs, such as those under EO 12333, were not ended. Narrowed to the bulk collection of phone records. The phrase 'debate that ended with the USA FREEDOM Act' was also recast so it no longer puts a causal sequence in the court's mouth.

fieldFixes.contribution: Snowden, a 29-year-old Booz Allen Hamilton employee working at the NSA and a former CIA technical assistant, copied top-secret documents on US and allied mass surveillance at the NSA office in Hawaii, flew to Hong Kong on 20 May 2013, gave them to journalists he trusted and identified himself in the Guardian on 9 June 2013. The disclosures began with the bulk collection of Americans' phone records. A criminal complaint dated 14 June 2013 charged him with theft of government property and two Espionage Act offences; he has lived in Russia since 2013 and was granted Russian citizenship by decree in September 2022.
fieldFixes.influence: In the Ninth Circuit's words, his disclosure of the phone-records program 'prompted significant public debate'; in June 2015 Congress passed the USA FREEDOM Act, which the court said 'effectively ended' the NSA's bulk collection of phone records, and in 2020 the same court held the program had exceeded the authority Congress gave.
